extracted.intended_audience: judges, patent attorneys, inventors, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing whether a patent specification sufficiently discloses an invention — i.e., whether a person of ordinary skill can make and use the invention without performing inventive work or undue experimentation, and whether the inventor disclosed known best modes and necessary particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate inventions must be supported separately
rubrics_metrics.description: If two inventions are put into one patent each must be supported as a separate patent; each invention must be useful and described so people clearly know what the invention is and how it is to be carried into effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Doctrine applied to each invention in the specification separately (example: steam-engine and machinery for propelling vessels in same patent must each be sufficiently specified).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement — specification must enable a competent workman
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must describe the invention so as to enable any one to know what he has invented and to enable a workman of competent skill to carry the invention into effect without any new invention or addition of their own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may call upon a workman to exercise ordinary existing knowledge common to the trade, but you cannot call upon him to tax his ingenuity or invention; if ordinary competent engineers could apply their skill and previous knowledge to construct the invention from the specification, the specification is sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must be full, fair, open, and sufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: The public have a right to expect and require that the specification shall be fair, honest, open, and sufficient; the patentee should communicate what the public are entitled to receive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentee should not be allowed to state a specification so that, after the patent term, the public cannot carry the invention into effect because the inventor 'kept his secret.' Avoid captious objections that do not go to the merits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must not cast expense or labour of experiments on the public
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification that casts upon the public the expense and labor of experiments and trials is bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: patent for drying malt that said degree of heat 'will be easily learned by experience' was criticized; spec must save the public the trouble of making experiments and trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode / disclose particular modes known to inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: If a patentee is acquainted with any particular mode by which his invention may be most conveniently carried into effect, he ought to state it in his specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: omission to mention use of tallow where inventor used it rendered specification bad; bound to make bona fide full and candid disclosure of known favorable practices or parameters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not merely set a problem — teach the method of doing it
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must actually and plainly set forth what the invention is and how it is to be carried into effect, not merely suggest something that will set the mind of an ingenious man at work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the invention can only be carried into effect by setting persons a problem to solve (i.e., requiring invention by others), the specification is defective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings are illustrative, not limiting — but drawings alone may be insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: A drawing should be treated only as an illustration of the invention and not as confining the invention to a particular drawing; but if treated as only an illustration, the specification must supply directions enabling construction beyond the picture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the drawing were the sole criterion then to show infringement one would have to show identical conformity to the drawing; accordingly the specification must contain directions enabling construction in other forms or skilled person must be able to do it without additional invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must supply necessary dimensions and reasonable data
rubrics_metrics.description: If essential particulars (e.g., lengths of rods, position of eccentric center, diameters, immersion) are omitted and can only be ascertained by subsequent experiments, the specification is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasonable data that a constructor should require (such as wheel diameter and immersion of float) ought to be given; if particulars cannot be exactly ascertained they should at least be stated or a method for determining them indicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment standard — whether a person of ordinary skill can practice without invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The true criterion is whether a person of ordinary and competent skill, bringing ordinary knowledge to bear, would be able to practise the invention from the directions in the specification and drawing without having to make inventive discoveries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of witnesses that a competent engineer could construct the machine from the specification is material; however, exclude or discount testimony based on special knowledge acquired through involvement with the patentee or litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on expert testimony that reflects special knowledge from the case
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence should be evaluated with regard to whether the witness possessed only ordinary skill or had gained peculiar knowledge from making models or working under the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Testimony from persons who learned the method while making models for the patentee is less persuasive regarding whether the public could have used the specification at the time it was published.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on ordinary, likely cases — discard exaggerated or irrelevant extremes
rubrics_metrics.description: When judging sufficiency, discard exaggerated cases (e.g., impossible angles) and consider whether the information communicated would be enough in ordinary cases or in such cases as are likely to occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look to the substance of whether the specification would enable the invention in normal practice rather than edge or impossible scenarios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee must communicate all the knowledge he himself possessed
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patentee has given to the public all the knowledge he had himself about carrying the invention into effect, he has done what he ought to have done.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the practical test of satisfactory disclosure — the public should receive the inventor's own knowledge relevant to making and using the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight and classes of witnesses — practical artisans vs. scientific witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Both practical artisans (practical workmen) and persons with thorough theoretical scientific knowledge are appropriate witnesses, but they serve different purposes in showing novelty and sufficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts recognize both classes but assess their evidence differently; contradictions among scientific witnesses reflect genuine differences of opinion rather than corruption.
